title: The amazing disappearing exoplanet
gist: Hot Jupiter TOI-2535b, observed by TESS for about seven years, stopped transiting after its transit durations shrank, in the fastest inclination change observed for an exoplanet orbiting a single star. Modeling of 300,000 configurations suggests an unseen companion at least roughly Saturn-mass in orbital resonance with a modest mutual inclination, though how the system formed remains unexplained.

insights.claim: Hot Jupiter TOI-2535b, which orbits a K dwarf star every eight days and had been observed transiting for about seven years, has stopped transiting in the most recent observations.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Illustrates that exoplanet transit ephemerides can change, affecting telescope scheduling assumptions.

insights.claim: TOI-2535b's transit timing shifted by as much as six hours, a large variation for such a short orbit, indicating gravitational interactions with another planet not seen in TESS data.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Transit timing variations are a tool to infer hidden planets.
insights.locator: But a closer look at the data

insights.claim: TOI-2535b's transit duration grew progressively shorter, implying its path moved from crossing the star's equator to near a pole before it stopped transiting altogether.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.locator: The second oddity is that the transit duration

insights.claim: Researchers say TOI-2535b shows the fastest rate of orbital inclination change observed for an exoplanet orbiting a single star.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Record-setting result highlights unusual system dynamics.
insights.quote: “This is the fastest rate of inclination change observed for an exoplanet orbiting a single star.”

insights.claim: Researchers modeled 300,000 starting configurations, ran the best 100 forward a million years, and found about two-thirds became unstable, ruling out some orbital resonances.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Shows the compute-heavy modeling approach used to constrain unseen planets.

insights.claim: Surviving models require the unseen second planet to be at least roughly Saturn-mass with a limited angle between the two planets' orbits, since large angles lead to growing eccentricity and instability.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Provides target constraints for follow-up radial-velocity searches.

insights.claim: Radial-velocity data is not yet clean enough to detect the companion, and noise in transit timing means a third planet in the system cannot be excluded.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.so_what: Further observations needed; result remains provisional.
insights.locator: While a second planet hasn’t been detected

insights.claim: Disk-driven inward migration of giant planets should limit the angle between their orbits, so without some additional disruptive event it is unclear how the TOI-2535 system reached its current misaligned state.
insights.speaker: John Timmer
insights.locator: The question we probably can’t answer
